 Dónal Lunny, the musician who played a vital role in Irish music
 Updated / Friday, 23 Oct 2026
 16:33
 Dónal Lunny RIP 
 Niall Keegan
 By Niall Keegan 
 University of Limerick
 More from
 University of Limerick 
 Profile: 'It would be difficult to identify another figure who has had such a pivotal and influential role in shaping and developing folk and trad' 
 Dónal Lunny , who has died aged 79 , played a crucial role in the revival of traditional Irish music and the development of the Irish folk scene over the past six decades. It would be difficult to identify another figure who has had such a pivotal and consistently influential role in shaping and developing these genres.
 His life story is the story of Irish music for over the last half-century. Raised in Newbridge, Co. Kildare, he became a close friend and collaborator with Christy Moore while at school. He went on to study at the National College of Art and Design , Dublin, and throughout this period, he developed his musical skills, performing in several notable early folk and ballad bands such as the Rakes of Kildare (with Christy), The Parnell Folk, and Emmet Spiceland .

 With Emmet Spiceland, Lunny had his first significant success and established himself in the Dublin ballad scene of the late 1960s and early 1970s, working with other significant artists such as Andy Irvine and Mick Moloney. This period perhaps reached its culmination with the recording of Christy Moore’s second album, Prosperous , which laid the foundations of what is now considered one of the first 'supergroups’ of Irish traditional music, Planxty .
 Up to this point, it was rare to find organised ensemble performances of traditional Irish music designed for a listening audience. Most bands playing this music were either ceili bands, primarily playing traditional music in the context of dance, or ballad-focused bands influenced by the ground-breaking work of the Clancy Brothers and other ballad bands since the 1960s.
 Seán Ó Riada is often credited with making the first considered moves towards instrumental music for listening to (taking the model for performance from Classical and Jazz musics), but it was the innovative work of Lunny and his peers who brought traditional dance music and Ireland’s song traditions into a unified practice of music for listening to, taking models of performance from popular and folk music from the US and the UK.

 The first obvious instance of this was Planxty, which went through many personnel changes from 1971 to 1983. This is a project that Lunny kept returning to (most recently in a reunion release and tour in 2004). By combining the more folk and song-oriented talents of Christy Moore and Andy Irvine with the dance music royalty of piper Liam O’Flynn (seen by many as the natural successor of the great piper and traditionalist, Séamus Ennis ), this group was consolidated by the mediating talents of Lunny, who created a seamless connection between the song and the tune. This work of mediation has been a central tenet of Lunny’s musical contributions ever since.
 Lunny’s other great legacy ensemble was the (in)famous Bothy Band . Formed in 1974, lasting for five years and three studio albums, this is the band that has perhaps had the most impact on the world of instrumental traditional dance music - their tunes and arrangements continue to be a mainstay of the different contexts in which Irish traditional music is played around the world.
 This band saw the full integration of the tune and the song into the ensemble model for traditional Irish music, paving the way for most traditional bands that followed. The prodigious talents of instrumentalists such as Matt Molloy (flute), Tommy Peoples (fiddle), Paddy Keenan (uilleann pipes), and Kevin Burke (fiddle) were enhanced through the accompaniment of Lunny, with Mícheál and Tríona Ó Domhnaill who also brought their Donegal repertoire of English and Irish language songs.

 However, Lunny's reputation was made in roles often seen to be peripheral in the world of traditional music. He is not regarded primarily as a singer or a tune player (although he is known to do both) but as an accompanist, particularly on the bouzouki. It is obvious that Lunny played a central role in the acquisition and adaptation of this exotic, Grecian instrument into Irish tradition.
 With his work in the Bothy Band and Planxty, Lunny gave this new instrument a traditional voice whose authenticity remains largely unquestioned to this day despite its recent acquisition – a fact born of a style of accompaniment on the instrument which is deeply grounded in the rhythmical structures of what is fundamentally dance music. It is his rhythmic aesthetic, bound in a harmonic framework, that is perhaps fundamental to his style. This approach to rhythm also led him to experiment with the bodhrán.
 Lunny’s role as a peerless accompanist was just part of a larger musical personality that has enabled some of the most innovative and influential ensemble work in the contexts of traditional music and folk since the 1970s. He was a facilitator – bringing together musicians from diverse genres with apparently seamless outputs, creating new avenues for musical creativity through diverse musical communities.

 He became a pillar in the professionalised traditional music ensemble tradition, more recently performing with ensembles such as Coolfin , Usher's Island , and musicians such as Zoë Conway and Máirtín O’Connor. He had a significant reputation in terms of drawing together ensembles that unite diverse traditions, perhaps most notably Moving Hearts , which stitched together aspects of trad, folk rock, and jazz in the development of a more electric sound. Lunny’s reputation as a collaborator, musician, and producer across genres was peerless, working with musicians such as Shaun Davey, Micheál Ó Súilleabháin, Kate Bush, Paul Brady, Elvis Costello, Baaba Maal, Mick Hanly and many others.
 Lunny’s influence has crossed genres and generations. His pervasiveness comes not from his position as a tradition bearer, virtuoso musician, or innovative composer (although he is certainly all of these) but from his role as a superb and peerless facilitator. Music is fundamentally a communal and human activity, and his great talent was that he could bring people and communities together and draw new, ground-breaking art and music from that meeting. This is only made possible through an immense generosity of spirit, honesty, and work ethic that is recognised by all who have known him and worked with him.
